items.definition: a talk in which someone explains information to a group of people, often using slides
exampleSentences: She gave a presentation on the company's new products.
His presentation lasted about twenty minutes.

items.definition: the group of people who watch or listen to a talk, film, or performance
exampleSentences: The speaker asked the audience a question at the start.
A nervous presenter often avoids looking at the audience.

items.definition: one page of a presentation, usually shown on a screen
exampleSentences: Keep the text on each slide short and simple.
She moved to the next slide and showed a chart.

items.definition: a printed page given to people in an audience with information from a talk
exampleSentences: He gave everyone a handout with the main points.
The handout included a summary of the figures shown on screen.

items.definition: a short general description of something, without a lot of detail
exampleSentences: She began with an overview of the whole project.
Let me give you a quick overview before we look at the details.

items.definition: a short description of the main points of something
exampleSentences: He shared an outline of his talk before he began.
The outline helped the audience follow the structure of the presentation.

items.definition: to draw special attention to something important
exampleSentences: The chart highlights the busiest months of the year.
She highlighted three reasons for the change in strategy.

items.definition: the main speech at a conference or event, usually given by an important speaker
exampleSentences: The CEO delivered the keynote at this year's conference.
Her keynote inspired many people in the audience.

items.definition: an important idea or lesson that people remember after a talk
exampleSentences: The main takeaway from his talk was to keep things simple.
What's the one takeaway you want people to remember?

items.definition: to practice something, such as a speech, before doing it in front of people
exampleSentences: She rehearsed her presentation three times before the conference.
It helps to rehearse in front of a friend.

items.definition: to hold someone's attention and interest
exampleSentences: A good story can engage an audience quickly.
She used questions to engage the room from the start.

items.definition: the act of looking directly into another person's eyes while speaking
exampleSentences: Maintaining eye contact with the audience builds trust.
He kept glancing at his notes instead of making eye contact.

items.definition: a movement of your hands or arms that expresses a meaning or feeling
exampleSentences: She used a simple gesture to point at the chart.
Too many gestures can distract the audience.

items.definition: the speed at which someone speaks or does something
exampleSentences: Slow down your pace when you reach an important point.
Nervous speakers often talk at a fast pace.

items.definition: a word such as 'um' or 'like' that people repeat without meaning while they think of what to say next
exampleSentences: Try to avoid filler words like 'um' when you speak.
She removed most of the filler words after watching a recording of herself.

items.definition: a small card with a few words to remind a speaker what to say next
exampleSentences: He glanced at his cue card to remember the next point.
Cue cards work well if you don't want to read from a full script.

items.definition: sure of yourself and your abilities, without seeming nervous
exampleSentences: A confident speaker looks at the audience, not the floor.
She sounded more confident after weeks of rehearsing.

items.definition: a smooth move from one point or slide to the next
exampleSentences: Use a short sentence as a transition between slides.
A clear transition helps the audience follow your structure.

items.definition: a short piece of text marked with a small symbol, used to list separate points
exampleSentences: Keep each bullet point short and clear.
The slide had five bullet points instead of full sentences.

items.definition: a picture, chart, or object used to help explain something to an audience
exampleSentences: A chart is a simple visual aid for showing change over time.
He used a short video as a visual aid during his talk.

items.definition: a general direction in which something is changing
exampleSentences: The chart shows a clear trend over the past five years.
She explained the main trend before looking at individual numbers.

items.definition: changing at a constant, even rate, without sudden jumps
exampleSentences: The graph shows a steady rise from January to June.
Sales have grown at a steady pace this year.

items.definition: sudden and large, especially describing a change
exampleSentences: There was a sharp drop in numbers after the launch.
The chart shows a sharp increase in the final quarter.

items.definition: happening slowly over a period of time, not suddenly
exampleSentences: The improvement was gradual rather than immediate.
A gradual increase is easier to manage than a sudden one.

items.definition: very sudden, noticeable, and surprising
exampleSentences: The slide showed a dramatic change in customer numbers.
Her tone became more dramatic as she reached the final point.

items.definition: large or important enough to be noticed
exampleSentences: There was a significant difference between the two groups.
The results show a significant improvement over last year.

items.definition: to change often, moving up and down
exampleSentences: Attendance at the workshops tended to fluctuate from month to month.
The numbers fluctuated before settling into a clear pattern.

items.definition: to stop increasing and stay at the same level
exampleSentences: Growth plateaued after the first year.
The line on the chart plateaus around the halfway point.

items.definition: to reach the highest point or level, before starting to fall
exampleSentences: Online orders peaked in December and fell sharply in January.
As you can see on this slide, visitor numbers peak at around midday.

items.definition: to give a short summary of what has already been said
exampleSentences: Let's recap the main points before we finish.
He recapped the previous slide before moving on.

lessons.title: Grammar: Comparatives and superlatives for trends

items.definition: how to compare numbers and describe trends using comparative and superlative forms
items.explanationTR:
When we describe charts and trends in a presentation, we often compare numbers using comparative and superlative forms.

• Comparatives (for two things or two points in time) usually add '-er' to short adjectives or use 'more' with longer ones:
  - This quarter's numbers are higher than last quarter's.
  - The new product line grew more quickly than the old one.
  - Sales in the north are lower than sales in the south.

• Superlatives (for three or more things, or the most extreme point) add '-est' or use 'most':
  - March was the busiest month of the year.
  - This is the most significant change we have seen so far.
  - The smallest increase was in the second quarter.

• Useful patterns for trends: 'a sharper increase than', 'the steadiest growth', 'far more dramatic than', 'by far the highest'.

Using comparatives and superlatives correctly helps an audience understand exactly how one number relates to another, instead of just seeing that numbers went up or down.

questions.prompt: This year's growth was ---- than last year's.
questions.explanationTR: Comparing two years needs the comparative 'faster'. 'Fastest' is a superlative, wrong for comparing just two things, and 'more fast'/'most fast' are wrong forms since 'fast' takes '-er/-est', not 'more/most'.

questions.prompt: Of all four regions, the north had ---- sales growth.
questions.explanationTR: 'Of all four regions' signals a comparison among more than two, so the superlative 'the highest' is needed. 'Higher'/'the higher' are comparatives, which only compare two things, and 'more high' is not a correct form of 'high'.

questions.prompt: The second quarter was ---- than the first.
questions.explanationTR: Comparing two quarters with 'than' needs the comparative 'stronger'. 'Strongest' is a superlative, and 'more strong'/'most strong' are wrong forms since 'strong' takes '-er/-est'.

questions.prompt: This is ---- increase we have recorded in five years.
questions.explanationTR: 'In five years' points to a comparison among many results, so the superlative 'the biggest' is correct. 'Bigger'/'the bigger' are comparatives for two items only, and 'more big' is not a correct form.

questions.prompt: The new dashboard is ---- to read than the old spreadsheet.
questions.explanationTR: 'Easy' is a two-syllable adjective ending in 'y', so its comparative is 'easier', not 'more easy'. 'Easiest' is a superlative, wrong for comparing just two things, and 'as easy' does not fit with 'than'.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly compares the three product lines?
options: Product C sold the better of the three product lines.
Product C sold the best of the three product lines.
Product C sold more good than the others.
Product C is selling gooder than the others.
Product C sold the goodest of all.
questions.explanationTR: 'Best' is the correct superlative of 'well/good' for comparing three or more things. 'The better of the three' uses a comparative where a superlative is needed, and 'more good', 'gooder', and 'goodest' are not standard English forms.

questions.prompt: Attendance this month was ---- than we expected.
questions.explanationTR: Comparing the actual result with the expectation needs the comparative 'lower'. 'Lowest' is a superlative, and 'more low'/'most low' are wrong forms since 'low' takes '-er/-est'.

questions.prompt: Out of everyone on the team, she gave ---- presentation.
questions.explanationTR: 'Confident' is a longer adjective, so its superlative is 'the most confident', not '-est'. 'More confident' is a comparative, wrong for comparing everyone on the team, and 'confidentest' is not a real word.

items.definition: A short transcript of a business presentation about regional sales trends, with eight questions

passage.title: A Presentation on Regional Sales
passage.body:
Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining today's session. My name is Elena Martins, and I lead the regional sales team. Over the next fifteen minutes, I will walk you through our latest results and explain the main trends behind the numbers.

Let's start with an overview. On this slide, you can see sales figures from our four regions: North, South, East, and West. As the chart shows, the North region had the highest growth this year, with a steady rise every quarter. The South region also performed well, though its growth was more gradual than the North's.

The East region tells a different story. Sales there rose sharply in the first quarter, then fell just as quickly in the second. This kind of fluctuation usually points to a single large order rather than a genuine change in demand, and our data supports that idea. By the third quarter, East had returned to a level similar to last year's.

The West region had the smallest increase of the four, but it was still positive, and the team there deserves credit for a difficult market.

I want to highlight one more point before we move on. When we compare this year with last year, overall growth was significantly higher, and customer satisfaction scores were also better across every region. That is the clearest sign that our new approach is working.

Now, let's look more closely at what made the North region so successful, and what the other regions can learn from it. I will keep this next part brief, because I know you are waiting for the question and answer session at the end, and I promise we will have plenty of time for that.

questions.prompt: Which region had the highest growth this year, according to the speaker?
questions.explanationTR: The speaker says the North region had the highest growth this year, with a steady rise every quarter. No other region is described as having faster growth.

questions.prompt: How did the South region's growth compare with the North's?
options: It was faster than the North's
It was more gradual than the North's
It was exactly the same as the North's
It declined while the North's grew
questions.explanationTR: The passage says the South region's growth 'was more gradual than the North's', meaning slower and steadier, not faster or equal.

questions.prompt: What most likely explains the East region's pattern of a sharp rise followed by a sharp fall?
options: A mistake in the sales data
A single large order rather than a real change in demand
A permanent decline in the market
A new competitor entering the region
questions.explanationTR: The passage explains that this kind of fluctuation 'usually points to a single large order rather than a genuine change in demand.' There is no mention of a data mistake, a permanent decline, or a new competitor.

questions.prompt: How does the passage describe the West region's result?
options: The largest increase of the four regions
A decrease compared with last year
No change from the previous year
The smallest increase of the four, but still positive
The region with the highest customer satisfaction
questions.explanationTR: The speaker states that the West region 'had the smallest increase of the four, but it was still positive,' ruling out a decrease or no change at all.

questions.prompt: According to the speaker, how did this year's overall growth compare with last year's?
questions.explanationTR: The speaker directly compares this year with last year and says overall growth 'was significantly higher,' not lower or unchanged.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say about customer satisfaction scores?
options: They were better across every region
They fell in every region except the North
They were unavailable for this year
They were the same as last year
They improved only in the North
questions.explanationTR: The passage says customer satisfaction scores 'were also better across every region,' not worse or unavailable, and not limited to one region.

questions.prompt: What will the speaker most likely talk about next?
options: The history of the sales team
What made the North region successful and what others can learn
questions.explanationTR: The speaker announces she will look at 'what made the North region so successful, and what the other regions can learn from it,' which is the clear next topic.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker say she will keep the next part brief?
options: She is running out of slides
She has technical problems with the projector
She was asked to finish early by her manager
She wants to leave time for the question and answer session
She thinks the audience is not interested
questions.explanationTR: The speaker explains she will be brief because the audience is 'waiting for the question and answer session at the end,' and she wants to leave enough time for it.
